how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Flooring bid calculator

How much should I charge for flooring installation?

A blended dollar-per-square-foot number is the flooring version of a postcard special: it prices the finished floor and ignores the two things that actually move the job — how much material waste the pattern creates, and how much of the room is tear-out instead of install. A straight-lay LVP room and a diagonal-pattern room the same size are not the same material order. A room with ceramic tile to demo first is not the same labor hours as one that's already down to subfloor.

Open the free flooring bid calculator

What a blended $/sq ft price cannot see

Waste. Straight-lay LVP commonly starts around 8% waste; diagonal or herringbone often needs 12% or more. That is material you buy and pay for, not extra floor the customer sees — and a quote that ignores it is quietly eating margin on every box.

Tear-out. Demoing ceramic tile can take more hours than laying new LVP in the same room. A quote that treats every room as "install only" underbids the ones that aren't.

Stairs. Stairs are priced per tread, not as hallway square footage folded into the total. Each tread is its own cut, its own nosing, its own labor.

A bid you can defend

  1. Price purchased material per room after your waste percent, not the finished square footage.
  2. Add demo hours for rooms that need tear-out, separately from install hours.
  3. Price stairs per tread.
  4. Load the wage (payroll burden), then add overhead, and price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin).

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. It is not a quote you can send as-is — it is a draft to check against your own invoices, payroll, and a walk-through before you send a price.

Worked example

A great room in straight-lay LVP at 8% waste and a stairway with a diagonal accent room at 12% waste are not one blended square-foot number — they are two different material orders. Add a kitchen where the existing tile has to come out first, and the labor hours split three ways before a single plank goes down. The calculator prices each of those separately, then rolls them into one job price and one price per installed square foot so you can see what the blended number was hiding.

Common questions

How much waste should I add to an LVP flooring bid?

Straight-lay LVP commonly starts around 8% waste; diagonal or herringbone often needs 12% or more. Waste is extra material you buy, not extra floor the customer sees. This calculator applies your waste percent to purchased square footage and underlayment, then shows the dollars that waste actually costs.

Why does a price per square foot underbid a kitchen or stairs?

Tear-out is a different job from the install. Ceramic tile demo can take more hours than laying new LVP in the same room. Stairs are priced per tread, not as hallway square footage. A blended $/sq ft on the finished floor cannot see either one.

Is this a quote I can send a customer?

No. It is arithmetic on the numbers you enter — a draft to check against your own invoices, payroll, and a walk-through. Copy the bid summary, then verify every figure before you send a price.

vs-a-flat-price-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Flooring Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per square foot

Flooring installers are shopped by a flat price per square foot. That rate cannot see the job — material, waste, tear-out, stairs, and leveling do not scale with finished square footage, and two jobs of the same size can take nearly nine times apart in labor.

What a flat price per square foot is

A price per square foot is the fastest number to quote over the phone: measure the rooms, multiply by a rate, read back a total. It is also the unit homeowners already compare between competing bids, and the unit most generic online flooring calculators hand back.

The rate behind it was learned from a specific job — a given material, a given tear-out, no stairs — and then reused for the next square footage that calls in, whether or not that next job shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter a room list with material, waste percent, and tear-out per room, plus stair treads, transitions, furniture moves, floor leveling, and baseboard, and your own wage, payroll burden, material costs, dump fee, travel, overhead, and target margin. It prices the material after waste, the tear-out, and every extra as their own hours and cost lines — for this job, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat per-square-foot rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for straight-lay LVP and porcelain tile, even though tile can install at a fraction of LVP's rate and cost several times as much per square foot. Prices each room's own material, waste percent, and install rate, so a tile room costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for tear-out at all — an empty room and a room with an existing tile floor to demo get the same rate. Prices tear-out hours and disposal separately per room, from a tear-out type you pick.
Has no line for stair treads, transitions, furniture moves, leveling, or baseboard. Prices each of those as its own hours and material, on top of the room square footage.
Bills waste inside the same blended per-square-foot number, if at all. Applies each room's own waste percent to purchased material and underlayment, and shows the dollars that waste costs.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per installed square foot and the walk-away price alongside the total, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same footage, two different jobs

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $2.40 material and $0.35 underlayment per purchased square foot, $28 hourly wage, 30% burden, $85 dump fee, $40 travel, 12% overhead, 25% target margin:

300 square feet of empty-room, new-construction straight-lay LVP, with no tear-out and no extras, takes 3.8 crew-hours and prices at $1,721.07 for the job — $5.74 per square foot.

The same 300 square feet of porcelain tile over an existing ceramic tile tear-out — with 13 stair treads, 6 transitions, two rooms of furniture to move, 80 square feet of leveling, and 140 linear feet of baseboard — takes 32.6 crew-hours, costs $3,311.73 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $4,415.64 — $14.72 per square foot. Quoting the harder job at the empty-room job's learned rate of $5.74 per square foot gives $1,721.07 for the same 300 square feet, which is $1,590.67 below the harder job's own break-even cost — before counting the $2,694.58 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 25% target margin. Identical square footage, roughly nine times the labor, and a rate learned on the empty room loses money the moment the crew opens the tile.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per square foot get a flooring bid wrong?

Because finished square footage only measures how much floor is visible when the job is done, not what it takes to get there. 300 square feet of empty-room straight-lay LVP with no tear-out takes about 3.8 crew-hours. 300 square feet of porcelain tile over an existing ceramic tear-out, with 13 stair treads, 6 transitions, two rooms of furniture to move, leveling, and baseboard, takes about 32.6 crew-hours -- the same footage, roughly nine times the labor, because material, waste, tear-out, and extras do not scale with square footage.

What does a flat per-square-foot rate usually miss entirely?

Material and install rate (porcelain tile installs at a fraction of straight-lay LVP's rate), waste percent, tear-out (an existing ceramic tile floor can take far more labor to remove than the new floor takes to lay), stair treads, transitions, furniture moves, floor leveling, and baseboard. A flat rate has no line for any of them -- it is one number learned on one job and reused for the next square footage that calls in.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs: 300 square feet of empty-room straight-lay LVP with no tear-out takes 3.8 crew-hours and prices at $1,721.07 -- $5.74 per square foot. 300 square feet of porcelain tile over an existing ceramic tear-out, with 13 stair treads, 6 transitions, two furniture-move rooms, 80 square feet of leveling, and 140 linear feet of baseboard, takes 32.6 crew-hours, costs $3,311.73 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $4,415.64 -- $14.72 per square foot. Quoting the tile-and-extras job at the empty-room job's learned rate of $5.74 per square foot gives $1,721.07 for the same 300 square feet, which is $1,590.67 below the harder job's own break-even cost -- before counting the $2,694.58 it falls short of this calculator's price at a 25% target margin.

Is a flat price per square foot ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- the same material, the same tear-out, no stairs or leveling -- a per-square-foot number can land close. The risk is quoting a harder material, an existing floor that has to come out, stairs, transitions, furniture moves, or leveling the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know any of that until the crew is on site, and by then the per-square-foot number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supplier's material pricing. It takes a room list with material, waste percent, and tear-out, plus stair treads, transitions, furniture moves, leveling, baseboard, your own wage, payroll burden, dump fee, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into crew hours and a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

vs-rfms.html.text:
← Flooring Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. RFMS

Two different shapes: RFMS is business-management ERP and takeoff software for running a flooring dealership. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this install cost, given its waste, tear-out, and stairs, before you open a dealership system.

What each tool is for

RFMS (Resource & Financial Management Systems, now operating as part of Cyncly) is business-management software built specifically for the flooring industry, in continuous use since 1984 and reported to run over 3,000 dealers across 7,000-plus locations. Its Core product unifies sales, inventory, purchasing, installation scheduling, and accounting into one dealership-wide system. A separate Measure product handles takeoff — drawing room diagrams, assigning products, optimizing seams and pattern layout to cut waste, allocating rolls, and calculating grout — and is built to hand a completed takeoff straight into Core as an order. It is sold as an ongoing dealer account. RFMS's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — flooring-specific dealer ERP plus a separate takeoff product, sold as a dealer account — are stated, and no dollar amount for RFMS appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what RFMS does. It does not manage inventory, purchasing, roll allocation, or installation scheduling across a dealership, and it stores no customer or job record. It takes one job's room list — material, waste percent, tear-out, and stair treads — plus crew wage, payroll burden, and target margin, and turns that into the purchased material after waste, the crew hours the job actually consumes, the price per installed square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a flooring dealership and need inventory, purchasing, installation scheduling, and accounting in one system across every job and every showroom.RFMS Core, or a comparable flooring-dealer ERP — running a whole dealership is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this one flooring install, given its waste, tear-out, and stairs, before I quote it?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
How much extra material does a diagonal or herringbone pattern actually need next to a straight-lay room?This calculator's waste-adjusted purchased material, not a blended per-square-foot guess.
Is the price I'm about to send still above my walk-away cost?This calculator's compare-to-proposed-price check.
I need room-diagram takeoff with seam, pattern, and roll-allocation optimization feeding straight into dealership orders.RFMS Measure, or a comparable flooring takeoff tool.
How does the math behind a per-job flooring price actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. RFMS is used through a dealer account.

Most flooring businesses get different value from each: RFMS (or a comparable dealer ERP) for running inventory, purchasing, scheduling, and accounting across a whole dealership as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login gut-check on what one install should cost from its waste and tear-out before a dealership system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed proposal, an invoice, or a site inspection.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or RFMS?

They do different jobs, and a flooring dealer of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. RFMS (Resource & Financial Management Systems, now part of Cyncly) is business-management ERP software built specifically for flooring dealers, in continuous use since 1984 and reported to run over 3,000 dealers across 7,000-plus locations. Its Core product unifies sales, inventory, purchasing, installation scheduling, and accounting for a whole dealership; its separate Measure product handles takeoff — room diagrams, seam and pattern layout, roll allocation, and grout calculation — typically feeding orders straight into Core. It is sold as an ongoing dealer account. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from a room list with material, waste percent, tear-out, and stair treads, plus crew wage, payroll burden, and target margin, it turns that into the purchased material after waste, the crew hours the job actually consumes, the price per installed square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before any of it touches a dealership system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A dealership that already manages inventory, purchasing, and installation scheduling across every job and every showroom is better served by RFMS or a comparable flooring ERP; an installer or small shop who wants an instant, private gut-check on what one job should cost from its waste and tear-out before opening a business system is in the right place here.
